requirements.requirement: Run a long-running background worker as a managed systemd service named inventory-worker on node1
requirements.summary: The unit /etc/systemd/system/inventory-worker.service was created with a continuous loop script (sleep 10 between ticks) and Restart=always, then enabled and started. systemctl status confirms it is loaded/enabled/active, and state.log shows repeated timestamped ticks proving continuous background operation both before and after a full node reboot.

requirements.requirement: Service is confined so it writes only inside /var/lib/inventory
requirements.summary: Using ReadOnlyDirectories=/ and ReadWriteDirectories=/var/lib/inventory (the systemd-219-era sandboxing directives, since ReadWritePaths/ProtectSystem=strict are unavailable on this systemd version), the service's mount namespace shows root mounted read-only with /var/lib/inventory as the sole read-write bind mount. Live tests as root inside the sandbox's mount namespace confirm writes outside /var/lib/inventory fail with 'Read-only file system' while writes inside succeed. This was re-verified identically on the new process after a full reboot.
NoNewPrivileges=yes is set in the unit and /proc/<pid>/status shows NoNewPrivs: 1 for both the original and the post-reboot service process.

overall_summary: The executor delivered a working, correctly hardened inventory-worker systemd service on node1: it is enabled/active, continuously appends timestamped ticks to /var/lib/inventory/state.log, is confined by a read-only root with /var/lib/inventory as the only writable mount, and runs with NoNewPrivs=1. All three material outcomes are directly demonstrated via mount-namespace inspection and live write tests, not just configuration inspection. The executor additionally ran the provider-wide reboot protocol, capturing a coherent pre-restart baseline, a differing boot_id after `systemctl reboot`, and confirmed the service, its data, and its sandbox confinement all survived and recovered post-reboot — this is not a stated task requirement but strengthens confidence that the setup is durable rather than a one-off configuration. Test artifacts created during verification were promptly cleaned up, and the one exception is captured inside a self-cleaning PrivateTmp mount.
limitations: Package-health checks were unavailable (timed out) in both before-prepare and after-executor snapshots, so native package consistency cannot be independently confirmed, though this is unrelated to the task's core requirements.

The reboot/restart evidence, while thorough and complete, is not itself a requirement of the stated task (which only asks for a confined managed service); it is treated here as supplemental confidence-building evidence per the provider-wide protocol rather than a scored material outcome.

operational_hygiene.summary: All state-changing executor commands map cleanly to the task: creating the inventory-worker user/directory, the worker script, and the systemd unit are all required deliverables. Several verification steps created small test files outside and inside /var/lib/inventory (ok-write, inside-sandbox-ok, confined-ok, /var/tmp/unconfined-test, post-reboot-ok); all were removed in the same or an immediately following command (cmd-7f3f7a1d845e4377 cleans up the pre-reboot test files, cmd-58aafb50912043f1 removes post-reboot-ok inline). One nsenter-created file (/var/tmp/inside-sandbox-test in cmd-7ff359b42a534d9d) is not explicitly rm'd, but it lives under the service's PrivateTmp bind mount, which systemd tears down automatically and is not visible on the real host filesystem, so it leaves no durable residue. The only broad state change is `systemctl reboot` (cmd-e4152b7a62714c0c), which is an intentional, required action for the independent restart-evidence protocol, not an unnecessary mutation. No failed/orphaned services, no weakened security controls, and no abandoned files are visible in the after-executor lifecycle snapshot beyond the expected new systemd-private tmp mounts tied to the running service.
